blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The standard deviation (SD) is the square root of the variance: σ = √σ² for a population, s = √s² for a sample. It is the root-mean-square deviation from the mean, expressed in the original units.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Variance squares the units (kg²), and nobody has a feel for “2.5 kg² of spread”. The square root returns to kg. Read an SD as a typical distance from the mean that gives large deviations extra weight. It is not the average distance from the mean: that is the mean deviation (§3.5), and the SD is always at least as large as the MD.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Five weights: s = √2.5 ≈ 1.58 kg. This is the root-mean-square distance from the mean. It exceeds the mean deviation (1.2 kg) because squaring gives the two children 2 kg from the mean more weight than the children 1 kg away.

Today’s 30 children: s = √3.07 = 1.75 kg (MD 1.41 kg).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: SD from grouped data
blocks.html:
With only the table, use mid-points x and frequencies f (grouped mean 11.8 kg, recall §2.2.1): s² = Σf(x − mean)² ÷ (N − 1).

Mid-point x f x − 11.8 (x − 11.8)² f(x − 11.8)²
9 5 −2.8 7.84 39.20
11 12 −0.8 0.64 7.68
13 9 1.2 1.44 12.96
15 4 3.2 10.24 40.96
Total 30 100.80
  1. s² = 100.80 ÷ 29 = 3.48 kg².
  2. s = √3.48 = 1.86 kg, against 1.75 kg from the raw data. Grouping moves every child to a class mid-point, and with these classes that slightly exaggerates the spread.

points.html: SD = √variance. The SD with divisor n is at least as large as the MD, equal only when every deviation has the same size; s, with divisor n − 1, is larger still.
The usual summary for roughly symmetric interval or ratio data is mean ± SD.

A large or small SD means something only relative to the variable’s scale: an SD of 5 is large for haemoglobin in g/dL and small for age in years. The coefficient of variation (§3.8) makes that comparison explicit.

The SD sets the spread (scale) of the Normal distribution (the bell-shaped curve of §5.7.2.2); every Normal curve has the same shape. It is also the building block of the standard error (§6.7) and of confidence intervals (§7.2).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 3.2

questions.prompt: Explain why variance squares the deviations instead of averaging them directly, and name one property squared deviations have that absolute deviations lack.
questions.answer: Raw deviations from the mean always sum to zero (Σ(x − x̄) = 0), so their average is zero for every dataset and says nothing about spread. Squaring removes the signs. Unlike absolute values, squares split cleanly: Σ(x − c)² = Σ(x − x̄)² + n(x̄ − c)² for any c. This identity shows that the mean minimises the sum of squares, gives the proof that E[Σ(x − x̄)²] = (n − 1)σ², and is the start of the sums-of-squares partitions used in ANOVA and regression.

questions.prompt: For the six haemoglobin values in Checkpoint 3.1 (9.0, 10.5, 11.0, 11.5, 12.0, 14.0 g/dL), compute the mean, the sum of squares, s² and s. Then compute SS ÷ n and say why it is not the usual estimate of σ².
questions.answer: Σx = 68.0; mean = 68.0 ÷ 6 = 11.33 g/dL. Σx² = 784.5; SS = Σx² − (Σx)² ÷ n = 784.5 − 4624 ÷ 6 = 784.5 − 770.67 = 13.83. (Directly: deviations −2.33, −0.83, −0.33, 0.17, 0.67, 2.67; squares 5.44, 0.69, 0.11, 0.03, 0.44, 7.11; total 13.83.) s² = 13.83 ÷ 5 = 2.77 (g/dL)²; s = √2.77 = 1.66 g/dL. SS ÷ n = 13.83 ÷ 6 = 2.31. Deviations are measured from x̄, the point that minimises squared distance, and on average over repeated samples E[SS] = (n − 1)σ². So SS ÷ n underestimates σ² on average by the factor (n − 1)/n = 5/6. Dividing by n − 1 removes that bias.

questions.prompt: A student writes: “SD = 1.66 g/dL, so on average each woman’s haemoglobin differs from the mean by 1.66 g/dL.” Correct the sentence, using the mean deviation of the same data.
questions.answer: The average absolute distance from the mean is the mean deviation: (2.33 + 0.83 + 0.33 + 0.17 + 0.67 + 2.67) ÷ 6 = 7.0 ÷ 6 = 1.17 g/dL. A correct sentence: “The SD is 1.66 g/dL, the root-mean-square distance from the mean. It gives the two women farthest from the mean (9.0 and 14.0 g/dL) extra weight, so it exceeds the mean deviation of 1.17 g/dL.”
